demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Negative Appraisals.value: I should have protected others and I failed
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'I have no future' is a broad, severe hopelessness appraisal, while 'others can see what happened to me just by looking at me' implies a visible stigma/marked external sign. For a trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another, the latter is hard to justify clinically unless there is disfigurement or public exposure, neither of which is represented elsewhere.

issues.item: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: For a male delivery driver whose trauma was accidentally causing serious injury to another person, the appraisal that others can visibly see what happened to him by looking at him is hard to reconcile with the trauma type unless there are visible injuries or marked stigma, which are not otherwise represented. The other selected appraisals centre on guilt and responsibility, so this item pulls toward a different formulation theme and is not well aligned with the otherwise coherent guilt-based negative appraisal pattern.

vignette:
Raj is a 34-year-old delivery driver living in a Chicago suburb with his wife and two young children. He came to therapy after his wife urged him, worried by how withdrawn he had become in the months since a single terrible afternoon in late November. Raj had been making his usual route when he rounded a blind corner in a residential area and struck a seven-year-old boy who had darted into the street after a ball. The boy survived, but with a traumatic brain injury that required multiple surgeries and left him with lasting deficits. Raj stopped the van immediately, called 911, and stayed with the child until paramedics arrived, holding pressure on the wound as he had been taught in a first-aid course years before. But none of that mattered to him now. What he remembered, what he could not stop remembering, was the moment of impact itself-the thud, the impossible stillness of the small body on the asphalt-and then the thought that followed: I should have been paying more attention. I should have seen him coming. I should have done something different.

In the weeks after the accident, Raj found himself unable to stop replaying that moment. The memory felt vivid and immediate, as though he were still in the driver's seat, still watching the boy step off the curb. He would be sorting packages in the back of his van and suddenly feel the steering wheel under his hands, hear the sound of the impact. At night, he woke in a cold sweat, convinced for a split second that he had just hit someone again. His wife would find him sitting on the edge of the bed, staring at the wall, and he would say only, "I can't stop thinking about it."

Raj had always been a careful driver, proud of his clean record and his ability to navigate the narrow streets of the older neighborhoods on his route. Now he found himself gripping the wheel so tightly that his hands ached by midday. He started taking longer routes to avoid the street where the accident had happened, adding twenty minutes to his shift. He began scanning the sidewalks with a hypervigilance that exhausted him, watching for children, for movement at the edges of his vision. He had come to believe that he could not trust himself behind the wheel, that his own judgment had failed at the critical moment and would fail again. Every school bus he passed, every playground he drove by, every child walking home from school made his chest tighten and his breath go shallow. He would pull over and wait until his heart stopped pounding, telling himself it was just a memory, it was over, but the feeling never quite went away.

At home, Raj had become quiet and irritable. He stopped playing with his own children, afraid that if he let himself feel too much joy, something terrible would happen again. He could not bear to watch them run in the yard, could not hear the sound of a ball bouncing on the driveway without flinching. His wife asked him why he seemed so distant, and he told her he was just tired from work, but the truth was that he could not forgive himself. He believed, with a certainty that felt like a physical weight in his chest, that he had failed to protect a child who had trusted the world to be safe, and that this failure could not be undone. He would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened, even though rationally he knew there had been no time, no warning, no way to see the boy before he appeared. The event happened because of the way he acted, he told himself. Because he was not paying enough attention. Because he was not good enough.

Six months after the accident, Raj was still avoiding that street, still scanning for children, still waking in the night. His supervisor had noticed that he was taking longer on his routes and had asked if something was wrong. Raj said nothing. But the pressure was building-at work, at home, in his own mind-and when his wife found him one evening sitting in the dark in the parked van, unable to come inside, she told him he needed to talk to someone. Raj agreed because he did not know what else to do, and because he was afraid that if he kept going like this, he would lose everything: his job, his marriage, his sense of himself as a good man. What frightened him most was the thought that he might never feel normal again, that this guilt would be with him forever, and that maybe-maybe-he deserved it.
